As early as 2024, the U.S. Department of Justice filed a lawsuit against Apple, accusing it of a "smartphone monopoly."

Over the past two years, Apple has repeatedly opposed the case. Now, a Bloomberg report indicates that the Department of Justice and Apple are in negotiations over a settlement.

According to Bloomberg, Apple has put forward "multiple proposals" this year in an attempt to settle the case:

The report also cautioned that although the negotiations are still ongoing, there is no guarantee that Apple and the Department of Justice will ultimately reach an agreement.

The antitrust lawsuit brought by the Department of Justice against Apple mainly revolves around five aspects of the iPhone user experience: super apps, cloud-streamed games, third-party messaging apps, third-party smartwatches, and third-party digital wallets.

Over the past year, Apple has indeed made some substantive changes in response to some of the Department of Justice's concerns, including supporting the RCS communication protocol in the Messages app, launching a new "Mini App Partner Program" in the App Store, and expanding access to the iPhone's NFC chip.

Whether these changes will satisfy the Department of Justice remains unknown. Admittedly, political factors are also involved, and Bloomberg offers the following analysis:

Apple and the Department of Justice recently submitted a joint progress report to the court, updating the latest developments in the case. In addition, Apple earlier this week also won an argument, blocking the Department of Justice's request to access federal government agency documents in the case.

9to5Mac Perspective

If Apple and the Department of Justice ultimately reach a settlement, it will significantly reduce the burden on John Ternus when he takes over as Apple's CEO in September.
